title: Recursion Tree Method
summary: Visual and algebraic method for solving recurrence equations by representing recursive calls as levels of a tree. Includes applicability, level construction, height, leaves, total sum, dominance patterns, and worked examples.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when it is convenient to use the recursion tree method, especially when the Master Theorem does not apply or when you want to visually justify the cost by levels.

terms.label: recursion tree
terms.definition: Representation of a recurrence as a tree where each node is a recursive call and each level groups subproblems of the same depth.

terms.label: Root
terms.definition: First node of the tree, corresponding to the original call T(n).

terms.label: Level
terms.definition: Set of recursive calls located at the same depth within the tree.

terms.label: Generic level i
terms.definition: Algebraic model that describes the behavior of any level i of the tree: number of nodes, input size and total cost.

terms.label: Leaves
terms.definition: End nodes of the tree where the base case of the recurrence is reached.

terms.label: Height
terms.definition: Number of reductions necessary to get from T(n) to the base case.

terms.label: Cost per node
terms.definition: Non-recursive work performed by a specific call. Normally it corresponds to f(subproblem size).

terms.label: Cost per level
terms.definition: Sum of the cost of all nodes located at the same level of the tree.

terms.label: leaf dominance
terms.definition: Case where the largest asymptotic contribution to the total cost comes from the leaves of the tree.

terms.label: root dominance
terms.definition: Case where the greatest asymptotic contribution to the total cost comes from the initial cost or from higher levels.

terms.label: Uniform cost per level
terms.definition: Case where all levels asymptotically cost the same, so the total cost is cost_per_level multiplied by the number of levels.

terms.label: Unbalanced recurrence
terms.definition: Recursion where the recursive calls have different sizes, for example T(n)=T(n/3)+T(2n/3)+cn.

chapters.title: Recursion Tree Method
chapters.summary: Construction, analysis by levels and resolution of recurrences through call trees.

sections.title: When does the tree method apply?

learningObjectives.text: Define the pedagogical applicability of the recursion tree method.
Distinguish when to use recursion tree instead of Master Theorem.

content.text: The recursion tree method represents a recurrence equation as a call tree. Each node represents a recursive call, each level represents an expansion depth, and the total cost is obtained by adding the cost of all levels plus the cost of the leaves.
It applies pedagogically to any recurrence equation, but is especially useful when the Master Theorem does not apply, for example in unbalanced recurrences such as
, or when the equation has more than one recursive call of different size.

learningObjectives.text: Interpret root, internal nodes, levels and leaves in a recursion tree.
Connect the recursion tree with the execution environments studied in recursion.

content.text: The root represents the first execution environment: the original call
. Its children represent the recursive calls that that root triggers. Each child spawns other children until the base case is reached.

blocks.title: What is paid at each node

content.text: The cost written inside a node is the non-recursive work: splitting, comparing, combining, printing, or executing local instructions. Recursive calls are not counted within
; They expand like children of the tree.

blocks.title: Generic level i model for balanced recurrences

learningObjectives.text: Classify the tree according to whether leaves dominate, uniform levels or roots.

content.text: After constructing the total sum, the decisive step is to identify which part of the tree dominates asymptotic growth.

cells.text: leaves dominate
The cost per level increases geometrically as you go down.
There are too many leaves or too much branching.
All levels cost the same
Each level costs, for example, cn.
The same cost is paid for each level and there are log n levels.
Master the root
Costs decrease rapidly as they go down.
The initial local work outweighs everything that happens underneath.

content.text: Don't decide the result by just looking at the number of leaves. A tree can have many leaves, but if the cost per level drops fast enough, the root can dominate. Always add or compare the cost by level.

steps.title: Observation

content.text: In unbalanced trees not all branches are the same height. For an initial explanation, it is enough to use the longest branch to limit the number of levels and observe that the cost per complete level is linear. For a fine formal proof, substitution or the Akra–Bazzi theorem is used, which is outside the scope of this module.
